Jack's Daily News

No. 19· 26 October 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. Meta booked a $9.89 billion charge for its teen-safety settlement this quarter and still grew advertising revenue 26% to $63.06 billion, almost entirely by raising prices rather than serving more ads (October 21 earnings).

  2. The same week, Netflix opened its own ad targeting to The Trade Desk's outside data marketplace and OpenAI widened ChatGPT ads from image generation into full conversations.

  3. NAB Show New York closed treating the creator economy as a main track, not a sideshow, and the one slice of streaming ad inventory still commanding a price premium is live content, exactly what a half-empty football stadium already proved in 1967.

The world

thedesk.net / ppc.land · October 21, 2026

Meta's ad business grows by raising prices, not serving more ads

Meta reported Q3 2026 earnings on October 21: total revenue $64.6 billion, advertising revenue $63.06 billion, up 26% from $50.08 billion a year earlier. The growth came almost entirely from price, not volume: ad impressions across Meta's apps grew just 10% year on year while the average price per ad rose 14%. In the US and Canada the gap was sharper, impressions up 8%, price up 23%.

Net income rose to $9.86 billion despite a $9.89 billion charge this quarter tied to the roughly $18.59 billion multistate settlement over teen mental health harms, the same case this brief first covered in issue 10. CEO Mark Zuckerberg tied the quarter to AI: “We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone, including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model.”

Why it mattersMeta isn't selling more ads, it's selling the same ads for more money. Raising price per ad by double digits in the same quarter it absorbs a $9.89 billion legal bill means advertiser demand for its inventory isn't just resilient, it's inelastic.
Bloomberg Law and others · October 13, 2026

OpenAI moves ChatGPT ads from image generation into the conversation itself

OpenAI announced on October 13 it will test contextually targeted ads inside ChatGPT conversations for US users, a wider step than the image-generation-only ad test this brief covered in issue 16. The new ads are triggered by conversation topic, not just an image prompt; OpenAI says conversation content won't train its models or be sold to advertisers, and it has built in blocks against showing ads during emotionally vulnerable conversations.

Eligibility is unchanged: only the free tier and the $8/month Go tier in the US see ads, Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise stay ad-free.

Why it mattersImage-generation ads were a contained experiment. Ads inside the conversation itself are the real monetization lever, OpenAI's version of what turned Google's answer box into inventory twenty-five years ago.
ppc.land / StreamTV Insider · October 20, 2026

Netflix lets outside data target its own ads, starting in November

Netflix and The Trade Desk announced that, starting in November, advertisers buying Netflix inventory through Trade Desk's Kokai platform can target audiences using their own first-party lists or third-party data from Trade Desk's marketplace of more than 300 suppliers. Until now, Trade Desk buyers could only use Netflix's own targeting; Amazon and Yahoo buyers already had outside data access.

Netflix paired this with a wider Ads Suite update: a new Netflix Pixel, an expanded Conversion API, in-DSP measurement inside Yahoo DSP, and 11 more countries getting the Netflix ad plan in March 2027.

Why it mattersThe same week a US judge is weighing how fast to force Google to open its ad exchange to outside bidders (see Radar), Netflix is opening its own targeting voluntarily. One platform is being ordered to interoperate, the other is choosing to, because buyers now expect it as the price of staying on the media plan.
nabshow.com / sportsvideo.org / radioink.com · October 21-22, 2026

NAB Show New York closes with the creator economy as a main track

NAB Show New York ran October 21-22 at the Javits Center: around 250 exhibiting companies (37 first-timers), more than 150 speakers, attendees from close to 100 countries. Day one centered on AI and big media; day two was built around creators and streaming, with sessions like “Scaling Your Creator Business” covering how creators build structure, ownership and long-term value around their audience and IP, alongside panels on brand deals, equity partnerships and IP ownership.

It's the third time this brief has tracked the creator economy move from side conversation to scheduled track at a legacy broadcast event (issues 12 and 16).

Why it mattersA trade show built for broadcast engineers now runs a full day on how one creator turns an audience into owned equity. The infrastructure of “old media” events is being rebuilt around people who never touched a broadcast license.

Campaigns & brand moves

hyundai.news / affaritaliani.it · October 22, 2026

Hyundai takes the IONIQ 3 launch out of car advertising entirely

Hyundai Italy launched its national campaign for the all-electric IONIQ 3 on October 22 under the line “Nuova forma alla libertà” (A new shape for freedom), built around daily life rather than range or specs: time for trips, people, passions. The rollout avoids traditional car-ad placements: a presence inside the OASIS Live 25 documentary on Disney+, a cinema run from October 22 to November 4 across 1,359 Italian screens, and digital/social activity through November 27.

It converges on an Open Weekend, October 24-25, when the car is shown in Hyundai's own showrooms, backed by a financing offer advertised as “Yours from 300 euros a month” over 35 installments. One detail in the campaign's own key visual: it carries a small “AI Generated” label in the corner.

Why it mattersPutting a car campaign inside a Disney+ documentary instead of a car-show stand is a bet that EV attention now lives in lifestyle content, not automotive content. The quiet “AI Generated” disclosure on the hero image is the more interesting signal: Italian advertising is starting to label synthetic creative as routine, not controversy.
press.wolt.com · October 15, 2026

A delivery app turns itself into a full commerce-media network

Wolt Ads, part of the DoorDash-owned commerce-media network that also includes Deliveroo, announced four ad-tech partnerships at once on October 15: Koddi, letting agencies activate Wolt campaigns from platforms they already use like The Trade Desk; Magnite, whose streamr.ai tools let brands build connected-TV and streaming ads in minutes; Skai and StackAdapt for search and social amplification; plus an expanding fleet of branded electric delivery vehicles as a scalable out-of-home format.

Together they let a brand's Wolt campaign follow a customer off the app, onto CTV, into search, and out onto the street. Deliveroo Media, launched in 2025, now reaches more than 56 million monthly active users across more than 40 countries as part of the same DoorDash-led network.

Why it mattersA food-delivery app just assembled the same off-platform, cross-channel stack that took Amazon and Walmart years of retail-media investment to build, by partnering instead of building. Commerce media is now a plug-in business model, not a years-long infrastructure project.

What is working in content

CTV industry benchmarks / exchange4media · 2026

Streaming ad prices are falling everywhere except where the content is live

Connected TV ad inventory has surged across the market in 2026, pushing blended CPMs down toward a market average around $26, most campaigns landing between $25 and $35. The one category moving the opposite direction is premium live content: India's IPL season this year held CTV placements at roughly ₹21 lakh (about $23,700) against ₹18 lakh for linear TV in the same slots, a premium that has only grown as bundled CTV-plus-TV deals scale.

NAB Show New York's own programming (News, above) pointed the same way, naming live shopping and social-first series as where attention is actually moving, not on-demand catalog content.

Why it mattersWhen supply is abundant, price should fall, and mostly it does. The exception is anything that happens once, live, and can't be rewound, exactly the quality Meta's rising price-per-ad and Netflix's new targeting tools are both trying to manufacture synthetically. Scarcity, not reach, is what buyers are actually paying for.

The historical bridge

Los Angeles, 1967

The game nobody wanted to watch invented the most expensive 30 seconds in advertising

Super Bowl I, played January 15, 1967 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum between the Green Bay Packers and Kansas City Chiefs, didn't even sell out: the Coliseum's upper deck was tarped off, and tickets sold for as little as $6 went unclaimed. CBS and NBC both carried the game, under separate rival contracts with the NFL and AFL. A 30-second commercial that day cost advertisers $42,000.

There was nothing scarce about the game itself. What was scarce was the moment: a single live broadcast, watched at the same time by everyone who cared, with no way to see it later. That scarcity is the entire reason the price climbed, almost without interruption, to $222,000 by 1980, $1.1 million by 1995, $4.5 million by 2015, and an average of $8 million in 2026, with a handful of spots clearing $10 million for the first time ever.

Why it still holds. Meta just raised its average price per ad 14 to 23% while the number of ads it actually served grew by single digits (News, above). CTV pricing is falling everywhere except live, appointment content (Content, above). Fifty-nine years apart, the mechanism is identical: a half-empty stadium in 1967 and an oversupplied streaming market in 2026 both prove that price was never really about how much inventory exists. It's about how much of it can't be replayed.
